attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post, stated as his own claim.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the AAAI survey, the majority, the 'wide margin' threshold and the broad-sample scope. It correctly leaves out the inference about LeCun's isolation.

contract.note: Reading 'doubting LLMs can reach AGI' as doubting that scaling current approaches reaches AGI is an ordinary reading in this scaling context. 'Wide margin' is left without a numeric cutoff, and 'broad sampling' is not treated as a representative sample. Both are fair.

evidence.note: Dated March 2025, before the post. It reports that 76% of AAAI survey respondents rated scaling current approaches to AGI unlikely or very unlikely, from a sample of 475 across academia and regions.

reviews.rationale: Before the post, the AAAI 2025 survey reported that 76% thought scaling current approaches was unlikely or very unlikely to yield AGI. That is a clearly substantial majority, from respondents in several settings and regions. This meets the support condition. The exact count answering this question is not given, but that does not undercut the majority finding.

contract.note: The criteria for a qualifying acknowledgement (naming Marcus and affirming he was right) match the plain words. The contract also correctly holds that a search finding nothing cannot prove 'never'.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no evidence items. The searches found no qualifying acknowledgement, but the contract says a search finding nothing is not enough to support 'never', and the record searched is admittedly incomplete. Nothing contradicts the claim either, so it is unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The proposition faithfully restates the historical claim. It drops 'as noted here a few months ago', which changes nothing.

contract.note: The broad reading of world models as symbolic cognitive representations matches Marcus's own 'world (cognitive) models' framing. It is an ordinary reading. 'Goes back to' is not read as a claim that GPS came first.

evidence.note: McCarthy and Hayes (1969), a scholarly technical account, cite GPS to Newell et al. 1959. They describe it as representing problems as symbolic expressions transformed by fixed rules, i.e. an internal problem representation with transformations.

reviews.rationale: A scholarly account tied to the 1959 publications shows that GPS existed in the 1950s and reasoned using an internal symbolic representation with transformation rules. This meets the contract's support condition under its fair, broad meaning of world model. The claim does not assert that GPS is the same as modern learned world models.

evidence.note: Ha and Schmidhuber's 2018 World Models shows earlier work on one theme. It does not establish priority across all five or how often LeCun credits others.
In a 2022 thread LeCun said many of the ideas in his proposal were not new and not his. This is a general acknowledgement that names no one, so it settles neither part of the claim.

reviews.rationale: Priority was not established for all five ideas, and there was no representative attribution audit. The evidence covers only parts of the world-models theme, plus one general acknowledgement by LeCun. Neither part of this compound claim is settled.
